query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, whose overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior across different temperatures remain unclear, what single intervention could improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions, defines the operating limits of the prediction, cites supporting evidence from the introduction, and proposes a falsification experiment capable of resolving microscopic deformation during wear.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix can be improved by introducing a surface modification, such as a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy film, which can provide a protective layer against wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.intervention: Introduction of a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy film
generation.conditions: Sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths
generation.mechanism: The nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy film provides a protective layer against wear and corrosion, which can improve the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating. The film's high hardness and strength, attributed to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening, can also contribute to the improved wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.baseline: Unmodified FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.boundary: Operating limits of the prediction: temperature range, friction velocity range, and wear depth range
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in the prediction due to the complexity of the high-entropy alloy system and the variability of the processing conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear test with varying temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear resistance of the modified FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating is not improved compared to the unmodified coating, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
